groups.title: One-to-one
groups.description: Account and Profile: where the foreign key lives and why it is unique.

groups.title: Owning side and mappedBy
groups.description: Department and Employee: which Java reference actually decides the foreign key.

groups.title: Many-to-many
groups.description: Student and Course: the join table and its owning side.

groups.title: Cascade and orphanRemoval
groups.description: Three isolated parent and child pairs mapped three different ways.

groups.title: Lazy and eager fetching
groups.description: When related data is loaded, and what happens when the session is already closed.

groups.title: The N+1 query problem
groups.description: Count the real statements, then reduce them with JOIN FETCH and an EntityGraph.

groups.title: Persistence context and dirty checking
groups.description: Entity states, the first-level cache, flush and commit.

experiments.title: Where does the foreign key go in a one-to-one?
experiments.question: Persist an Account with its Profile, read the rows back, then try to give the account a second profile.
experiments.claim: The foreign key column is in the table of the owning side (jpa_lab_profile.account_id), it is UNIQUE, and MySQL refuses a second profile for the same account.

experiments.title: Set only the owning side
experiments.question: What if the employee points at the department but the department's list is not updated?
experiments.claim: The foreign key is written, but the department's in-memory collection stays out of date.

experiments.title: Change only the inverse collection
experiments.question: What if you add the employee to department.getEmployees() and nothing else?
experiments.claim: The foreign key stays NULL: modifying the inverse collection never changes a foreign key.

experiments.title: Update both sides with a helper method
experiments.question: What if department.addEmployee(employee) sets both references?
experiments.claim: The foreign key is written and both Java sides agree.

experiments.title: How is a many-to-many stored?
experiments.question: Enroll one student in two courses, then withdraw from one.
experiments.claim: The owning side writes one join table row per course, and withdrawing deletes only the join row, never the course.

experiments.title: Change only the inverse side of a many-to-many
experiments.question: What if you add the student to course.getStudents() and flush?
experiments.claim: No join row is written until the owning collection is changed.

experiments.title: Persist a parent without cascade
experiments.question: What does persist(department) do to an employee that is only in the department's collection?
experiments.claim: Only the department is persisted; the employee is a separate entity that cascade does not reach.

experiments.title: Persist a parent with cascade ALL
experiments.question: What does persist(project) do to its tasks when the association has cascade = ALL?
experiments.claim: Hibernate inserts the project and then each task, with project_id set.

experiments.title: Update a managed parent
experiments.question: What SQL does changing a managed parent's field produce, and are its children touched?
experiments.claim: One UPDATE of the parent row at flush; no save() call and no statement for the children.

experiments.title: Remove a child from the collection (cascade ALL, no orphanRemoval)
experiments.question: Does removing a task from project.getTasks() delete the task?
experiments.claim: No SQL is produced and both task rows remain: cascade and orphanRemoval are different things.

experiments.title: Remove a child from the collection (orphanRemoval = true)
experiments.question: Does removing a member from team.getMembers() delete the member?
experiments.claim: Hibernate prepares a DELETE for the removed member.

experiments.title: Remove a parent that has children and no cascade
experiments.question: What happens when you remove a department whose employees still reference it?
experiments.claim: Hibernate prepares a DELETE for the department and MySQL refuses it because of the foreign key.

experiments.title: Remove a parent with cascade ALL
experiments.question: What happens when you remove a team whose members cascade?
experiments.claim: Hibernate deletes the members first and then the team.

experiments.title: Load an entity and never touch its collection
experiments.question: What SQL runs when you load a department but do not use its employees?
experiments.claim: Only the department is selected; the lazy collection stays uninitialised and no employee statement is prepared.

experiments.title: Touch a lazy collection inside the transaction
experiments.question: What happens when you call getEmployees().size() while the persistence context is open?
experiments.claim: A second SELECT loads the employees, filtered by the foreign key.

experiments.title: Touch a lazy collection after the session closed
experiments.question: What happens when the department is used after its transaction ended?
experiments.claim: Hibernate throws LazyInitializationException and prepares no statement; this application keeps Open Session in View off.

experiments.title: What are the real fetch defaults?
experiments.question: Compare a @ManyToOne with no fetch attribute and one marked LAZY.
experiments.claim: @ManyToOne defaults to EAGER (the project is loaded with the task); @OneToMany defaults to LAZY; the explicit LAZY reference is a proxy.

experiments.title: Is EAGER the cure for lazy loading?
experiments.question: Load every task with a JPQL query when Task.project is EAGER.
experiments.claim: No: Hibernate issues one extra SELECT per distinct project, so EAGER can itself cause N+1.

experiments.title: Experiment A: the N+1 problem
experiments.question: Load departments, then use each department's employees. How many statements run, and how does that change with N?
experiments.claim: 1 statement for the departments plus one per department; the total grows with the number of departments.

experiments.title: Experiment B: JOIN FETCH
experiments.question: Load the same departments with a JPQL fetch join and compare the statement count.
experiments.claim: One statement loads the departments with their employees, and using the employees afterwards costs nothing.

experiments.title: Experiment C: EntityGraph
experiments.question: Load the same departments with an @EntityGraph on the repository method.
experiments.claim: One statement fetches the employees together with the departments, without changing the JPQL.

experiments.title: Fetching two collections at once
experiments.question: What does one join fetch of both employees and rooms cost the database?
experiments.claim: One statement, but the database returns employees times rooms rows per department, far more than the objects needed.

experiments.title: Transient, managed, detached, removed
experiments.question: Walk one entity through persist, detach, merge and remove and watch what the EntityManager reports.
experiments.claim: contains() is false for new, true when managed, false after detach, merge returns a different managed instance, and remove deletes at flush; with IDENTITY persist() runs its INSERT immediately.

experiments.title: Dirty checking, flush and commit
experiments.question: Change a managed entity's field without calling save, then flush, then commit.
experiments.claim: No SQL at the change, an UPDATE at flush, and another transaction sees the new value only after commit.

experiments.title: The first-level cache
experiments.question: Call find() twice, run a query for the same row, then clear the persistence context.
experiments.claim: The second find() prepares no statement and returns the same instance; a query still reads the database but returns the same instance; after clear() the row is read again.

limitations: SQL shown is the text Hibernate handed to JDBC, with ? placeholders. It does not show bound values, the rows MySQL returned or how MySQL executed the statement.
Rows shown were read with plain JDBC, which Hibernate never sees. Rows read inside the experiment transaction are visible to that transaction only until it commits.
Every experiment works on its own temporary rows in the jpa_lab_* tables and removes them afterwards. No application table is read or changed.
Statements issued by the lab's own verification reads (plain JDBC) are not Hibernate statements and are not counted.
Behaviour described is that of the Hibernate and MySQL versions this application runs on; other versions or dialects may differ.
